guide.title: Period 9 (1980–present): review guide
guide.intro: Since 1980, a resurgent conservative movement, the end of the Cold War, a globalizing technology-driven economy, and new waves of immigration have reshaped the United States, which has faced new challenges after September 11, 2001. Causation is the period's key reasoning skill.

sections.title: Reagan and conservatism
body: A conservative coalition of free-market advocates, anticommunists, and religious conservatives (such as the Moral Majority) elected Ronald Reagan in 1980. Reagan cut income taxes, reduced regulation, and argued that big government was more a problem than a solution, though federal deficits grew as military spending rose.

Conservatives also emphasized traditional values and patriotism, as in Reagan's warnings about losing “the American memory.” Debates over the size of government and cultural values continued in later decades.
points: Contextualization: the 1970s' inflation, energy crises, and loss of confidence helped conservatives win.
Reagan's coalition joined economic and social conservatives.

sections.title: The end of the Cold War and new challenges
body: Reagan's military buildup and his later diplomacy with Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, along with the Soviet Union's internal economic and political problems, contributed to the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the collapse of the Soviet Union (1991).

After the September 11, 2001, attacks, the United States launched a war in Afghanistan and, in 2003, invaded Iraq, arguing that it possessed weapons of mass destruction; none were found. Debates over the wars, civil liberties, climate change, and economic crises such as the Great Recession (2008) marked the new century.
points: Causation: both U.S. pressure and Soviet internal problems ended the Cold War.
Officials' predictions about Iraq proved far too optimistic.

sections.title: A changing economy, migration, and immigration
body: Manufacturing jobs declined as the economy shifted toward services and technology; globalization and trade agreements such as NAFTA (1994) increased trade, and income inequality grew. Population and political power shifted toward the Sun Belt.

Immigration, especially from Latin America and Asia (encouraged by the 1965 immigration law), changed the nation's demographics and prompted debates over immigration policy, including the 1986 Immigration Reform and Control Act.
points: Immigration made the United States more diverse and became a lasting political issue.

example.prompt: Explain one cause of the end of the Cold War.
example.solution: The Soviet economy stagnated and could not keep up with U.S. military spending, and Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost and perestroika) loosened control, which allowed Eastern European revolutions in 1989 and led to the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991.

misconceptions: Soviet economic problems, Gorbachev's reforms, and Eastern European movements were also crucial.
“Conservatism in the 1980s was only about economics.”
It also stressed traditional moral and cultural values.
Manufacturing jobs declined as a share, while output and services grew.
Since the 1970s, most immigrants have come from Latin America and Asia.

passages.title: Source A: President Ronald Reagan, Farewell Address, 1989
text: “Those of us who are over thirty-five or so years of age grew up in a different America . . . We were taught, very directly, what it means to be an American. And we absorbed, almost in the air, a love of country and an appreciation of its institutions. . . . The movies celebrated democratic values and implicitly reinforced the idea that America was special. . . . I’m warning of an eradication of the American memory that could result, ultimately, in an erosion of the American spirit.”
passages.attribution: President Ronald Reagan, Farewell Address to the Nation, January 1989. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 31.2.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/31-2-political-and-cultural-fusions); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Statements by U.S. officials before the Iraq War, 2002
text: President George W. Bush, October 2002: “facing clear evidence of peril, we cannot wait for the final proof—the smoking gun—that could come in the form of a mushroom cloud.”
Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld, November 2002, on how long a war would last: “Five days or five weeks or five months, but it certainly isn’t going to last any longer than that.”
passages.attribution: Public statements by President George W. Bush and Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld, 2002. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 32.1.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/32-1-the-war-on-terror); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of the changing economy since 1980
text: “The American economy of the early twenty-first century looked very different from that of 1970. Factory jobs, especially in the industrial Midwest, declined as companies automated and moved production abroad, while employment grew in services, health care, finance, and technology. Tax cuts and deregulation, beginning in the 1980s, were meant to unleash growth, and the economy did grow, but the gains went disproportionately to those at the top. A college degree became more important than ever to earning a middle-class income.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of immigration since 1965
text: “The Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas of the 1920s, and its effects reached far beyond what its sponsors predicted. In the decades that followed, most immigrants came not from Europe but from Latin America and Asia. Immigrants built businesses, revitalized city neighborhoods, and filled jobs from agriculture to engineering. Their arrival also sparked recurring political battles over undocumented immigration, border security, and what it means to be American.”
